Kiran Bazaar: Predicting Next-Month Food Price Spikes in Pakistan

CT-378 Machine Learning · Semester Project · Group: [names / roll numbers] · November 2026

Abstract

Food inflation is one of the most pressing household problems in Pakistan. We frame it as a binary classification task: will the retail price of a staple in a given city rise by more than 5 % next month? Using WFP / Pakistan Bureau of Statistics monthly prices for 13 staples in 5 cities (2014-2026, 9,633 city-item-months), combined with fuel, labour-wage and implied exchange-rate series, we engineered 26 leakage-free features and compared nine course algorithms under a chronological split with 5-fold time-series cross-validation. A Random Forest, selected on validation and probability-calibrated (Platt scaling), reached ROC-AUC 0.83 and F1 0.48 on the held-out 2024-26 test period, against 0.61 / 0.33 for a persistence baseline. The model is deployed as a Streamlit app, a Hugging Face Space with model card, and a Flask REST API with an HTML front end.

1. Problem and motivation

Between 2022 and 2024 Pakistan's food prices rose faster than at any time in the dataset: atta in Lahore roughly tripled from its 2021 level at the 2023-24 peak. A household, NGO or ration-distribution programme that knew a month ahead that "atta in Lahore has a high chance of jumping next month" could buy early or pre-position stock. Most prior ML work on this data predicts the price level (regression). We instead predict the event that matters to users: a spike above 5 % (≈ 15 % of city-item-months). This gives a clear target, meaningful metrics (F1, ROC-AUC) and an actionable output. A companion regression model supplies the expected next-month price.

2. Data collection

WFP Markets for Pakistan (HDX)market → province, district, latitude, longitudeCC BY-IGOretrieved 2026-11-18

We combine (i) the 13 food series (targets), (ii) the diesel, petrol and unskilled-wage series as cost-push drivers joined by city and month, (iii) a monthly USD/PKR rate implied by WFP's own conversion (Σprice / Σusdprice) and (iv) the market table. Data are market-level aggregates with no personal identifiers. The modelling window starts in 2014-01: before that only rice and wheat exist and the fuel/wage series are empty. Final table: 9,633 labelled rows × 26 features (4 categorical, 22 numeric) + 5 derived in-pipeline.

3. Exploratory data analysis

Fig. 1 - National price index of staples vs implied USD/PKR.
Fig. 2 - Spike rate by commodity and by year (class balance).

Seven EDA plots are in notebooks/01_eda.ipynb: coverage/missingness heatmap, distributions, trends, outliers, class balance, correlations, seasonality. Key findings: (1) prices are right-skewed and trend strongly with the rupee, so we use percentage changes rather than levels; (2) 40-50 % of months are missing for staples that start in 2013-15, and internal gaps are imputed inside the pipeline; (3) poultry and eggs spike 35-40 % of months while oil, ghee and milk rarely do; extreme changes are genuine market events and are kept; (4) the target is imbalanced (15 % positive) and its rate shifts over time (18 % in the 2023-24 validation period, 13 % in test); (5) the best single correlates are recent volatility and national momentum (Spearman ρ ≈ 0.29), so signals must be combined; (6) poultry and eggs are clearly seasonal.

4. Methodology

  • Features (past-only): 1/2/3/6/12-month changes, 6-month volatility, price vs 3/12-month mean and 12-month high, spikes in last 12 months, gap vs other cities, national momentum of the item, city food-basket momentum, diesel/petrol/wage changes, USD/PKR 1/3-month changes, city, province, category, month. Level features (log-price, PKR level) were tried and removed: they trend for 20 years and made linear models extrapolate (validation ROC-AUC of logistic regression rose from 0.51 to 0.71 after removal).
  • Pipeline (fitted on training data only): DerivedFeatures (cyclical month, relative momentum, fuel pressure, acceleration) → ColumnTransformer [median imputation + missing indicators + StandardScaler | most-frequent imputation + one-hot] → model.
  • Split: chronological 70/15/15 on whole months. Train 2014-01 to 2022-12 (6,711 rows), validation 2023-01 to 2024-10 (1,427), test 2024-11 to 2026-09 (1,495).
  • Models: baselines (class prior; persistence rule "jumped last month") + Logistic Regression, PCA+LR, KNN, Gaussian Naive Bayes, SVM (RBF), Decision Tree, Random Forest, Bagging, Gradient Boosting. Regression: Linear, Ridge, RF and Gradient Boosting regressors.
  • Tuning: GridSearchCV / RandomizedSearchCV with 5-fold TimeSeriesSplit, scored on ROC-AUC; class_weight="balanced" for imbalance. The best model on validation ROC-AUC is chosen.
  • Calibration: class weighting inflated the forest's probabilities (validation: mean prediction 44% vs actual spike rate 18%), so the selected model is wrapped in CalibratedClassifierCV (sigmoid / Platt, 5-fold TimeSeriesSplit): validation Brier score 0.204 → 0.132, mean prediction 18%. The decision threshold is set on the calibrated validation probabilities to maximise F1 (0.22, not 0.5); the model is refit on train+validation and evaluated once on test.
  • Unsupervised (notebook 03): PCA (10 components for 90 % variance), K-Means on per-series volatility profiles (k = 4) and Apriori association rules on monthly co-spike baskets.

Over/under-fitting. KNN (train ROC-AUC 1.00 vs val 0.70) and Gradient Boosting (0.96 vs 0.74) over-fit. Logistic Regression and Naive Bayes show small gaps but low training scores (high bias, under-fitting). Random Forest and Bagging (both 0.93 vs 0.75) are essentially tied; by the pre-defined rule (highest validation ROC-AUC) Random Forest is selected (0.751 vs 0.750). Its remaining over-fit is limited by min_samples_leaf=25 and max_depth=16. The higher spike rate in validation (18 % vs 15 %) explains part of the gap between CV and validation scores.

Error analysis. The final model catches 66% of test spikes with 38% precision, versus 32%/33% for persistence. Its strongest signals are the national momentum of the item, its own last-month change and its recent spike history. Per commodity, test ROC-AUC is best for Oil (cooking) (0.80), Lentils (moong) (0.88), Lentils (masur) (0.92) and near chance for Eggs (0.57), Beans(mash) (0.57), Wheat flour (0.60). (Masoor daal's high score rests on a single test spike.) Part of the pooled 0.83 therefore comes from separating volatile from stable items. Fuel and FX features had near-zero or slightly negative importance on 2024-26, when the rupee was stable. Regression: the Gradient Boosting regressor reaches test MAE 3.46 pp (R² 0.054) vs 3.56 pp for "no change". Monthly changes are close to a random walk, which supports the classification framing.

6. Deployment

Fig. 8 - Streamlit app: probability, verdict, expected price, history and "why" charts.
Fig. 9 - Hugging Face Space (Gradio).
Fig. 10 - Flask app (POST /predict + HTML front end).

All three apps share src/kiranbazaar/inference.py and load the same joblib pipelines. The user picks a city, a staple and an "as-of" month, and can optionally override this month's price change, diesel change and USD/PKR change for what-if analysis. Each app returns the spike probability, a verdict at the tuned threshold, the expected next-month price and a local explanation: the change in probability when each feature is reset to its median. The Flask API validates inputs (unknown city/commodity, bad month format, out-of-range or non-numeric overrides, non-JSON body) and returns HTTP 400 with a readable message. The front end also validates fields before sending.

7. Limitations and future work

  • Only five large cities and monthly granularity. Weekly PBS SPI data would allow earlier warnings and more cities.
  • No exogenous shock features (floods, wheat support-price announcements, import duties, bird-flu outbreaks, Ramadan/Eid shifting through the calendar).
  • Regime shifts change the base rate (15 % → 18 % → 13 %), so even calibrated probabilities drift: the model should be retrained and re-calibrated monthly as new data arrives.
  • Within-commodity skill is uneven. Per-commodity models or commodity-specific features (international palm-oil and wheat prices) are the next step.
